lead: Two prayers stand at the heart of today's readings. Paul prays with all his heart for his own people, Israel, that they may be saved. A father kneels before Jesus and begs, “Lord, have mercy on my son.” Both readings ask what true faith is: not a righteousness of our own making, but trust in what God does in Christ, even if that trust is as small as a mustard seed. The key words are righteousness and faith.

r.h: My heart's desire and prayer for them
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's long reflection on his own people. He has said that he has “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” in his heart for them (9:2), and he has listed with pride what belongs to them: “the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises” (9:4). He will end this section with hope: “all Israel will be saved” (11:26), for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). Today's verses must be read within that whole.
str: v. 1: Paul's prayer for their salvation.
v. 2: a zeal for God, but not enlightened.
v. 3: seeking to establish their own righteousness, not submitting to God's.
v. 4: Christ, the end of the law, so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.
kw: Paul knows this zeal from inside. He was once “far more zealous for the traditions of my ancestors” (Galatians 1:14), and “as to zeal, a persecutor of the church” (Philippians 3:6). He does not mock it; he honours it, and grieves that it has missed its goal.
God's own saving justice, by which he makes sinners righteous as a gift. “Their own” righteousness is one that a person tries to establish by his own observance.

The word can mean an end as a stopping point and an end as a goal. Catholic interpreters generally stress the second: Christ is the goal toward which the law was leading, and in him it is fulfilled (compare Matthew 5:17: “I have come not to abolish but to fulfill”).
vv: Brothers and sisters, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.
The first word Paul says about his people here is a prayer. That remains the Christian way to speak of the Jewish people.
I can testify that they have a zeal for God, but it is not enlightened.
“Not enlightened” is literally “not according to knowledge” (ou kat' epignōsin). Paul speaks with respect: he bears witness to their zeal before he names what is lacking.
For Christ is the end of the law so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.
“Everyone”: Jew and Gentile alike. A few verses later Paul says, “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all” (10:12).
ch: The Church reads these verses with the whole of Romans 9–11. She teaches that the Jews remain most dear to God because of their fathers, for he does not repent of the gifts he makes or of the calls he issues (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839), and she prays for the Jewish people as “the first to hear the word of God” (CCC 839). The Catechism quotes verse 4 when it teaches that Christ is the end of the law, because he alone teaches and bestows the justice of God (CCC 1953). Paul's prayer in verse 1 remains a model for the Church: to speak of others first in prayer.

r.h: Faith the size of a mustard seed
set: This scene follows straight after the Transfiguration (17:1–8). Peter, James and John have seen Jesus in glory on the mountain; at its foot the other disciples have failed to heal a boy. Mark tells the same story at greater length (Mark 9:14–29), with the father's cry, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24).

Matthew's word for the boy's illness, selēniazetai, means literally “moon-struck”, because people linked such seizures to the moon; the NRSV renders it “epileptic”. The Gospel speaks both of an illness and of a demon (17:18), in the language of its time. The Church today carefully distinguishes illness, which is the concern of medicine, from the presence of the Evil One, before any exorcism is performed (CCC 1673).
str: vv. 14–16: the father kneels; the disciples could not cure his son.
v. 17: “You faithless and perverse generation … bring him here to me.”
v. 18: Jesus rebukes the demon; the boy is cured at once.
vv. 19–20: “Why could we not cast it out?” Faith the size of a mustard seed.

¶ Verse 21 (“But this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting”) is missing from the oldest manuscripts and the NRSV gives it only in a footnote; it was probably added from Mark 9:29. The POC joins the end of verse 20 to the number 21.
kw: Matthew's favourite reproach to the disciples: the noun here, and the related adjective oligopistoi, “you of little faith” (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8). It is not no faith, but weak and divided faith, faith that looks at the storm instead of at the Lord.
Proverbially the smallest of seeds (13:31–32). Jesus does not ask for great faith but for real faith: a small seed that is alive can move what seems immovable.

The words echo the Song of Moses about Israel in the wilderness, “a perverse and crooked generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5). The reproach falls on the whole generation, the disciples included, and not on the suffering father.
vv: Lord, have mercy on my son,
The father's prayer is the prayer of every parent, and it is close to the Church's oldest cry, Kyrie eleison, which the Holy Qurbono repeats many times.
Why could we not cast it out?
The disciples ask in private. It is a model for bringing our failures to the Lord honestly.
if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move;
“Moving mountains” was a proverbial image for doing what seems impossible. The mountain of the Transfiguration stands just behind them.
ch: The Church sees in this Gospel the power of faith joined to prayer. Mark's form of the saying, “This kind can come out only through prayer” (Mark 9:29), and the later reading that adds fasting, have shaped the Church's practice of meeting evil with prayer and fasting. For the Syro-Malankara faithful the Apostles' Fast begins on Wednesday 16 June: a time to bring the “mountains” of our lives to the Lord in that spirit. The father also teaches parents to bring their children to Christ in prayer, even when others have failed to help.

qa: Does Jesus mean that with enough faith we can get anything we want?

No. Faith is trust in God, not power over him. Jesus himself prayed, “yet not what I want but what you want” (Matthew 26:39). The promise that “nothing will be impossible” rests on God, of whom the angel said to Mary, “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). Mustard-seed faith places the mountain in God's hands and leaves the way it moves to him.
study: Paul's first words about those who had not accepted Christ are a prayer. How do I speak of people who do not share my faith?
What “mountain” in my life or my family seems immovable? How can I bring it to the Lord with mustard-seed faith, prayer and fasting, as the Apostles' Fast draws near?
